book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: Female carrying a lump of wood for lighting, for example

definitions.note: halogen names a kind of lighting, as in halogen lamps

indicators.note: a creature carrying something holds it inside her, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
taken as written
a log is a lump of wood

explanation.surface: A woman lugging a chunk of firewood to make light, perhaps for a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: HEN holds A LOG to make HALOGEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Halogen lamps are a common type of electric lighting, so the word stands as an example of lighting.

clue.text: Calling leg ball in play?

indicators.note: letters put in play are free to move about, so these words get rearranged

parts.note: the three words used as letters

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator naming a delivery down the leg side while the ball is live.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket words (leg, ball, in play) all belong to the surface; 'in' is part of the letters to rearrange, not part of the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something a name and labelling it are synonyms: both mean attaching a description or title to it.

clue.text: One half-day in knockout dress!

indicators.note: in places the first pieces inside the letters for knockout

parts.note: the standard boxing abbreviation for a knockout
Roman numeral one
the first half of Monday

explanation.surface: Someone wears a stunning outfit for just half a day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knockout dress' reads as a stunning frock, but knockout is the boxing abbreviation that wraps the other pieces, and the definition is dress alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A kimono is a traditional Japanese robe, a long dress-like garment, so it is an example of a dress.

clue.text: How might one get winning hands?

definitions.text: How might one get winning hands?

parts.words: How might one get winning hands?
parts.note: surface reading: how to be dealt victorious cards in a game
setter's reading: hands that are attractive and charming, made so by a beauty treatment

explanation.walkthrough: Card players think of a winning hand; here winning means charming, and the hands are literal ones being tidied and polished.
explanation.definitionFit: A manicure is a cosmetic treatment of the hands and nails, which is how one would get attractive hands.

clue.text: Mediaeval banquet might offer corporate growth

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a feast laid out in the Middle Ages
second meaning: corporate here is from Latin corpus, body, so a bodily expansion

explanation.walkthrough: A spread is a lavish meal, so a Middle Age one is a mediaeval feast; corporate growth sounds like business expansion but means a body getting bigger.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-age spread is the familiar idiom for the paunch people tend to develop around the waist in their forties and fifties.

clue.text: New first for one who writes

parts.note: novel means new or original
first is written 1ST, with the figure 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A new top position for a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often read the digit 1 as the letter I, so 1ST for first becomes IST.
explanation.definitionFit: A novelist is an author of novels, so is someone whose job is writing.

clue.text: What a priest might wear for bed and stay uncovered?

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its covering, so only the inside letters of the word stay

parts.note: the inner two letters of stay

explanation.surface: Wondering what a cleric wears to bed and whether he stays under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: COT plus the middle of stay gives COTTA, a word few solvers know but one that is fair from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cotta is a short white surplice worn over a cassock by clergy and choristers, so it is a priestly vestment.

clue.text: New publication about contentious point

parts.note: re means about or concerning
an issue is a matter in dispute

explanation.surface: A fresh book or article arguing about a disputed topic.
explanation.definitionFit: A reissue is a book or record published again, a fresh edition of an existing work.

clue.text: Regrettably went back to the motorway for some sausage

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: alas is an expression of regret
the M1, Britain's first motorway, with the figure 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Someone sadly drove back to the motorway services for a sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the main motorway north from London; setters write it MI.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a cured, highly seasoned Italian sausage, so a portion of it is some sausage.

clue.text: Veal? Do it perhaps as a joint

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters might be arranged differently, so they are reordered

parts.note: the letters of these words

explanation.surface: A cook asks whether to prepare veal as a roasting joint.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint looks like a cut of meat to go with veal; it is the carpentry sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A dovetail is an interlocking woodworking joint shaped like a dove's tail.

clue.text: Quartet said to have made a prediction?

parts.note: a quartet is four, which sounds like fore
said and told both mean related in words

explanation.surface: Four people are reported to have forecast something.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, four told and foretold are the same, so the homophone is signalled only by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To foretell is to predict, so foretold is the past tense: having predicted or prophesied.

clue.text: Intercede, seeing back trouble is beginning to ease

indicators.note: back says the word that follows runs the other way

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict
taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of ease

explanation.surface: Someone steps in, noticing that a sufferer's back pain is starting to let up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back trouble' reads as a sore back, but back is the reversal signal for trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To liaise is to act as a go-between, which is close to interceding between two parties.

clue.text: Spring cleaned? Congratulations!

parts.note: a well is a spring of water
as in cleaned out: swindled, done

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who has finished their spring cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: Spring cleaned reads as the annual tidy-up; split it into spring (WELL) and cleaned, meaning done or cheated.
explanation.definitionFit: Well done is the everyday exclamation of praise for an achievement, the same as saying congratulations.

clue.text: Fascinated by alternative sleeping accommodation given to sailors

parts.note: ABs are able seamen
or introduces an alternative
a bed is where one sleeps

explanation.surface: Someone intrigued by the choice of bunks offered to a ship's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: Given to sailors puts the sailors first, so ABS leads the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorbed means completely engrossed, so its attention held as if fascinated.

clue.text: Effect renovations after destructive brush-fire

indicators.note: something destructive breaks things up, so the letters are wrecked and reassembled

parts.note: the letters of the word, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: Rebuilding work carried out after scrubland has burned.
explanation.definitionFit: To refurbish is to renovate and redecorate, which is to carry out renovations on a building.

clue.text: Herald in trouble for being uncompromising

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder, so they get rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A messenger is punished for refusing to bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' looks like one phrase; 'in' belongs to the letters, leaving trouble as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardline describes a firm, unyielding stance that refuses concessions, which is what uncompromising means.

clue.text: Do nothing, say, about a generation without heart

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the rest

parts.note: to state is to say
taken as written

indicators.note: losing its heart leaves only the ends of the word, its outer pair

parts.note: the first and last letters of generation

explanation.surface: An idler, perhaps, describing a whole generation as heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: Say here is a verb to be swapped for a synonym, not the 'for example' it seems to be beside the idler; that synonym goes around the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagnate is to stay inactive and make no progress, which is doing nothing.

clue.text: No duty for cab to drop one without charge

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it go, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: a cab is a taxi
Roman numeral one, the letter to remove
free means costing nothing

explanation.surface: A cabbie dropping off a passenger at no cost and paying no levy.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop reads as setting down a passenger; it actually removes I from TAXI.
explanation.definitionFit: Tax-free means exempt from tax, and a duty is a tax, so no duty applies.

clue.text: The quality of a bore?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the internal diameter of a gun barrel

explanation.walkthrough: A bore sounds like a tedious person; here it is the hole down a gun barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Calibre means both a level of excellence and the measured width of a gun's bore.

clue.text: Most peculiar, seeing just one

definitions.note: most here means very, not a superlative
definitions.meaning: first meaning: remarkably odd or unusual
second meaning: the grammatical number for one thing

explanation.surface: Strange that someone is dating only one person.
explanation.walkthrough: Most is read as 'very', so most peculiar is an adjective without the superlative sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Singular means both extraordinary or strange and, in grammar, referring to only one.

clue.text: Name a hand weapon that fires

parts.note: standard abbreviation for name
taken as written
the palm is the inner part of the hand

explanation.surface: Asking for a handgun that shoots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand weapon' reads as a pistol; hand only gives PALM, and the weapon is defined separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Napalm is jellied petrol used in incendiary bombs, so it is a weapon that starts fires.

clue.text: The perfect shoe for cattle crossing?

definitions.note: perfect is surface praise; the definition is the shoe

parts.note: an ox is one of the cattle
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: Recommending sturdy footwear for wading cows through a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: An ox ford is literally a cattle crossing, as in the city's name.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford is a classic laced leather shoe, a standard formal style of men's footwear.

clue.text: Happen only cowards could understand reasons at first!

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A jibe that something happening makes sense only to cowards.
explanation.definitionFit: To occur is to take place, which is what happen means.

clue.text: Democracy is about the people

parts.note: surface reading: a slogan that democracy serves the populace
setter's reading: the Latin origin, res publica, the public matter or affair of the people

explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin res publica, the people's affair, so this kind of state is literally about the people.
explanation.definitionFit: A republic is a state governed by elected representatives rather than a monarch, a form of democracy.

clue.text: Drill for dubious race tips

indicators.note: something dubious is not to be trusted as it stands, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A punter rehearsing shaky horse-racing tips.
explanation.walkthrough: PRACTISE is the British spelling of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill is to train by repetition, which is practising.

clue.text: 25' These lights are, we hear, found in distress sales

indicators.note: found in places one piece inside the following word
distress, read as a verb, means to batter and disorder, so the letters get mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: we hear says the word is taken by its spoken form as a letter name

parts.note: the word are is pronounced like the letter R

explanation.surface: Emergency flares, perhaps, turn up in bargain clearance sales.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray '25'' at the start is a scanning artefact. R goes into SALES and the whole is mixed up; distress sales looks like a fixed phrase but distress is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasers produce narrow, intense beams of light, so they are a kind of light.

clue.text: Pal up with bachelor — terribly refined!

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done very badly, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor
taken as written

explanation.surface: Making friends with a very posh single man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pal up with bachelor' reads as one phrase; the definition stops at with.
explanation.definitionFit: To befriend someone is to become their friend, which is palling up with them.
